chunks: "A 10x probe is a voltage divider built into the probe.
It has a 9 megaohm resistor in the tip, in series with the scope's 1 megaohm input, so the scope sees one tenth of the signal.
The scope is told it's a 10x probe and multiplies the display back up by ten, so I read the real voltage. Why bother? Because it makes the probe load the circuit much less.
Instead of 1 megaohm and maybe 100 picofarads, which is mostly the cable and scope input, the circuit sees about 10 megaohms and roughly 10 picofarads.
That matters at high frequency, where the capacitance is what loads the circuit. It also extends the voltage range by ten.
The divider has capacitance too, which would make it frequency-dependent, so there is a small capacitor across the 9 megaohm resistor.
When that capacitor is correct, R 1C 1 equals R 2C 2 , the division is 10 to 1 at every frequency.
That's what the compensation screw does, and why I check it on the scope's square-wave calibration output.
The cost is that the signal is ten times smaller, so noise from the scope is relatively bigger, and for tiny signals I might use 1x."
